results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long you must keep tax records**

* Keep any records that support an item of income or deduction on your tax return until the “period of limitations” for that return runs out. The period of limitations is the time the IRS has to assess additional tax or you have the time to amend the return to claim a credit or refund. The specific limits for different types of returns are listed in the IRS table of periods of limitations (see Table 3).  
  – Example: for most individual income‑tax returns the limitation is 3 years after the return is filed unless a larger error exists.  

* If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.  
  – (“Employment taxes. If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.”) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* Records that relate to property (e.g., to calculate depreciation, basis, or gain/loss when you sell or otherwise dispose of the property) should be kept **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property**.  
  – (“Assets. Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition.”) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* It is also advisable to keep copies of every filed tax return itself, as they are needed to prepare future returns and to calculate any amended return.  
  – (“Keep copies of your filed tax returns. They help in preparing future tax returns and making computations if you file an amended return.”) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Summary**:  
- For ordinary income‑tax items, retain records for the applicable period of limitations (usually 3 years, or longer if the tax under‑reported a significant amount).  
- For employment taxes, keep records for 4 years.  
- For property‑related records, retain them through the limitation period of the year you dispose of the property.  

These are the specific retention periods provided in the IRS guidance.

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **Monitor your business’s progress** – Good records let you see whether the business is improving, which items sell best, and what changes are needed, increasing the likelihood of success. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

2. **Prepare accurate financial statements** – Records are required to build income‑statement (profit‑loss) and balance‑sheet reports that help you manage the business and satisfy banks or creditors. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

3. **Identify the source of receipts** – When money or property comes in, records show whether the income is taxable or non‑taxable and separate business receipts from personal ones, which is essential for correct tax reporting. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **Track deductible expenses** – Recording expenses as they occur prevents you from forgetting them when you file the tax return, ensuring you claim all allowed deductions. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

5. **Prepare and support tax returns** – All items you report on your tax return must be backed by records. The IRS may inspect your books, and a complete set will speed up any examination. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

6. **Meet IRS retention rules** – The IRS requires records to be available for inspection. The same rules apply to electronic records that replace hard copies, which must keep the same level of detail and accessibility. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

7. **Provide evidence for business and non‑business purposes** – Besides tax needs, insurers, creditors, and other entities may require these records for longer than the IRS mandates. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

8. **Maintain proper bookkeeping systems** – Whether you use a single‑entry or double‑entry system, keeping journals, ledgers, checkbooks, and inventory summaries helps keep your books balanced and audit‑ready. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

9. **Include required supporting documents** – Acceptable statements from banks, credit cards, and electronic funds transfers must show the check number, amount, payee, and posting date, and should be accompanied by receipts, invoices, or sales slips to prove a deduction. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

10. **Adjust for inventory and specific business needs** – If you hold inventory, you must keep inventory records and use an accounting method that clearly reflects income. If the business has multiple entities, separate books are required. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

By keeping these records, you not only satisfy legal and tax obligations but also gain a clearer picture of your business’s financial health and operational efficiency.

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
The IRS lets you pick one of several accounting methods for a business, but you must use the same method for both calculating taxable income and keeping your books, and you normally choose it when you file your first business tax return (Schedule C with Form 1040). Here’s how to decide which one is appropriate for you: | Accounting Method | When it’s usually used | What it means | Key rules from the IRS docs | |-------------------|------------------------|--------------|-----------------------------| | **Cash method** | • Small‑to‑mid‑size businesses that do not keep inventory.
• Businesses that want the simplest record‑keeping and usually collect cash quickly. | Income is reported in the year you receive the money; expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year you pay them. | • You must use the cash method for both income and expense reporting unless you have inventory, in which case you must use accrual for the inventory portion (but the rules treat the whole method as cash if you mix the two) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).
• If you change to a different method later, you must obtain IRS approval by filing Form 3115 [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17). | | **Accrual method** | • Businesses that keep inventory of goods for sale.
• Businesses that want to match income with the expenses that created it. | Income is reported when earned, regardless of when paid; expenses are reported when incurred. | • If your business sells products or manufactures goods, you generally must keep an inventory and use accrual for purchases and sales of inventory [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).
• Inventory includes goods held for sale, raw materials and supplies that will become part of merchandise, etc. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) | | **Special or combination methods** | • When you need to treat certain items differently (e.g., bad debts, depreciation, installment sales, long‑term contracts).
• When you use a mix of cash and accrual to get the best picture of your income but keep the method consistent. | You can combine elements of cash, accrual, and special methods, provided the combination clearly shows your income. | • If you mix cash and accrual, the combination is treated as cash for reporting purposes [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).
• Special methods (depreciation, amortization, depletion, etc.) are allowed for particular items and are explained in detailed IRS publications [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17). | | **Special small‑business exceptions** | • Small trade or business taxpayers with inventory production costs under $200 000 and no other disqualifying property. | You may opt out of the inventory‑accrual requirement and use the cash method even if you keep inventory. | • This exemption is listed under the uniform capitalization rules; it applies only to small‑business taxpayers and only when indirect production costs are ≤$200 000 [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17). | **How to choose:** 1. **Look at what your business sells**. * If you sell products and keep inventory of those products, you’re normally required to use the accrual method for those inventory transactions (unless the small‑business exception applies). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) * If you provide services and have no inventory, the cash method is usually simplest and acceptable. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) 2. **Consider how you receive money**. * If you get paid when the work is done, an accrual method will match income to the payment period. * If you get paid quickly and not much is owed to you, a cash method will show your cash flow accurately. 3. **Think about record‑keeping**. * The cash method needs less detailed inventory tracking and is easier to maintain for a single‑entry book‑keeping system. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) * The accrual method requires double‑entry bookkeeping or a detailed inventory and sales tracking system. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) 4. **Decide now and stick with it**. * Pick your method on your first income‑tax return (Schedule C). * If you later wish to change, you must file Form 3115 for approval (or rely on an automatic change if it applies). [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) **Bottom line:** - If you’re a small service‑based business that doesn’t hold inventory, the **cash method** is almost always the easiest and most appropriate choice. - If you sell products and keep inventory, you probably need the **accrual method** (unless the small‑business inventory exemption applies). - Either way, keep the same method for all income and expense reporting, and use the combination rules only if you truly need a mix. If you’re unsure whether your business meets the small‑business inventory exemption or how to account for a particular item (e.g., depreciation, bad debts), you can open the corresponding IRS publication (Pub. 538 for accounting methods, Pub. 946 for depreciation, etc.) or consult a tax professional. **Sources:** 1. results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the two‑step process outlined in the handbook:

**1. Conduct a routine self‑inspection**  
- **Use the handbook’s checklists** to look for common hazards in your industry. The checklists are a starting point for identifying what might be wrong and where to start fixing it. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
- **Record findings** on the same form, noting whether hazards were found, how they’re being controlled, and whether controls are still working. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
- **Involve workers**. Workers help spot hazards, suggest controls, and can be assigned to implement and evaluate those controls. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  

**2. Analyze and act on the results**  
- **Match any identified hazards to OSHA standards** that apply to your business. If a standard covers a hazard, follow its requirements; if it doesn’t, use the general‑duty clause. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)  
- **Compile all data** (checklists, injury/illness records, training logs, maintenance records) to see where the problems cluster. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
- **Find solutions**. Once you know where hazards exist, look to the handbook’s “additional resources” links or OSHA’s website for control options. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

**Additional support**  
- If the self‑inspection shows many hazards or you’re uncertain about compliance, **contact an OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program**. Consultants can help you identify hazards and fix them. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)  

**Keep the program ongoing**  
- Perform self‑inspections regularly; update your hazard list and controls as work or equipment changes.  
- Review the safety post‑on itself: keep the OSHA poster, notice of any citations, and emergency numbers posted. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=13)  

By following these steps—planning, inspecting, analyzing, acting, and repeating—you’ll maintain a safer workplace and stay in line with OSHA guidance.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash accounting and accrual accounting are the two main ways you can report business income and expenses for tax purposes.

**Cash method**

- You report income when you actually receive the money (or it becomes available to you – “constructive receipt”).  
  *Example:* a client sends a check on December 30 2024 that you get on January 4 2025 is counted as 2025 income [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you actually pay them.  
- It is the simpler method and is permitted for many sole proprietors who don’t keep inventory. However, if you have inventory you’re required to use accrual to record sales and purchases of that inventory but you can still use cash for other income and expenses that don’t involve inventory [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

**Accrual method**

- You report income in the year it is earned, even if the payment comes later, because the earning “events have occurred.”  
  *Example:* you sell a computer on December 28 2025, bill the customer in early January 2026, and get paid in February 2026, but the computer sale is 2025 income because the sale event happened in 2025 [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses in the year they are incurred, regardless of when you pay them.  
  *Example:* you buy office supplies in December 2025, receive the bill and pay it in January 2026, but you can deduct the expense in 2025 because the liability was fixed and economic performance occurred that year [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
- Accrual is required when you keep an inventory of goods, raw materials, or supplies that you intend to sell, because you must match the cost of those items with the revenue they generate [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) and also covered in Segment 4.

**Key differences summarized**

| Item | Cash method | Accrual method |
|------|-------------|----------------|
| Income timing | when money is received or constructively available | when earned (sales are made, services performed) |
| Expense timing | when money is paid | when incurred (purchase of goods, services, or capital) |
| Inventory requirement | not required for most sole‑prop businesses; if you have inventory, use accrual for those items | required for any business with inventory; inventory must be recorded at both the beginning and end of the year |
| Example of constructive receipt | a check sent December 30 but received January 4 is still 2025 income | – |
| Example of income earned but payment late | – | a December sale of computer counted in 2025 even if paid 2026 | 

These rules are the ones the IRS uses to let you pick the method that best matches how your business operates. If you keep inventory, you normally must use accrual; otherwise you can choose cash unless the IRS has a reason to require the other method.

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes – you can deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while you’re traveling for business.  
The deduction covers several categories of cost:

* **Meals and lodging** – If the trip is overnight or long enough that you need to sleep to perform your work, you may deduct the cost of meals and lodging.  You can use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance.  For most meals you may deduct only **50 %** of the cost【Segment 1】.  Lodging can be fully deducted if it is for a business trip【Segment 1】.  
* **Car and truck expenses** – Any rental car you use while away from home can be deducted in its entirety, but only for the portion used for business.  For your own vehicle you may deduct either the actual cost of operation (fuel, maintenance, insurance, parking, tolls, etc.) or the standard mileage rate.  For 2025 the standard mileage rate is **70 ¢ per business mile**【Segment 5】.  
* **Other transportation** – Taxi, commuter‑bus, limousine fares and other local transportation between the airport (or train station) and your hotel, or between the hotel and your work location, are deductible【Segment 3】.  
* **Telephone, fax and other communication** – Phone calls made for business while traveling are deductible【Segment 1】.  
* **Tips** – You may deduct tips paid for any service that appears in the travel‑expense list【Segment 1】.  
* **Baggage and shipping** – Sending baggage, samples or display material between your regular and temporary work locations is deductible【Segment 3】.  

If you reimburse employees for these travel expenses, the amount you reimburse can be deducted, but the manner of deduction depends on whether the reimbursement is under an accountable or non‑accountable plan (see Pub. 15)【Segment 1】.  

All deductions must be ordinary and necessary, and any personal portion of the expense must be separated and is not deductible (e.g., commuting miles to a regular place of business)【Segment 1】【Segment 5】.

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
**What goes in an executive summary**

- Keep it short: one or two paragraphs.  
- Give the reader an overview of **what you want to accomplish**.  
- Include the main points of the business plan:  

  1. **Your idea** – what product or service you’re offering.  
  2. **Funding needs** – how much money you need, what you’ll use it for, and how much you have already invested.  
  3. **Brief schedule of goals** – key milestones and when you expect to reach them.  

- Write this section **last**, after the rest of the plan is finished.  

These elements give a clear, concise snapshot of the business and its objectives.

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market clearly, follow the guidance below:

1. **State the market niche** – briefly say what type of customers you are focusing on.  
   Example: “We serve mid‑size tech companies in the East Coast region that need customized cybersecurity solutions.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **List the key characteristics of that customer** – break it down by one or more segmentation bases:
   - **Industry or business type** (e.g., software, manufacturing, healthcare)  
   - **Company size** (e.g., revenue, number of employees)  
   - **Geographic location** (city, state, region)  
   - **Product or service use** (who actually uses the product and why) – e.g., “IT managers who require 24‑hour remote support.”  
   - **Demographic or psychographic traits** (age, gender, lifestyle, values) where relevant for consumer markets.  
   Example: “IT managers aged 30–45, tech‑savvy, who prioritize data protection.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Estimate the target market’s size and growth potential** – use population data, industry listings, or sales tax records to quantify how many potential customers fit the niche.  
   Example: “There are about 400 mid‑size tech firms in New York and New Jersey that match our criteria, with an annual growth rate of 3 %.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Project how much of the market you plan to capture** – give a realistic percentage based on your product’s differentiated value, competitive analysis, and pricing strategy.  
   Example: “We aim to capture 10 % of the East Coast mid‑size tech market within five years.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Tie it into your business plan** – use the target market description in the marketing section to detail promotion, distribution, and service methods that appeal to those customers.  
   Example: “Our promotion will focus on industry‑specific trade shows and online webinars designed for IT managers.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

By following these steps you produce a concise, data‑driven description that clarifies who your best customers are and how you will reach them.

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  The ADA requires that businesses which open to the public remove physical barriers that are “readily achievable” and provide at least one accessible entrance and path of travel into the shop.  A shop must therefore make itself wheelchair‑accessible if the barriers can reasonably be removed.

* The ADA definition of “readily achievable” applies to any access barrier: if it can be removed with minimal difficulty or expense, the business must do so.  “If you own or operate a business that serves the public you must remove physical “barriers” that are “readily achievable.”” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
* An inaccessible turnstile or entrance must be replaced, removed, or an alternative accessible entrance provided if it is readily achievable.  “If an inaccessible turnstile is located at the entrance … it must be replaced or removed or an alternative accessible entrance provided … if doing so is readily achievable.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  
* A shop must have at least one accessible entrance.  “If a business has two public entrances, in most cases, only one must be accessible.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
* In addition, the shop’s interior path, aisles and counters must satisfy the ADA’s accessible‑route and accessible‑surface standards (e.g., a 36‑inch‑wide path and a 30‑by‑48‑inch clear floor area around an accessible counter) [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

So, if you serve the public, you are required to make your shop wheelchair‑accessible or remove the barriers that prevent wheelchair use.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You **do** have a specific exemption under OSHA’s injury‑recordkeeping rules, but only under certain conditions:

1. **Employee‑count exemption** – If you had **10 or fewer workers at every point of the last calendar year**, you are *partially exempt* from keeping the OSHA 300, 300A and 301 logs. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
2. **Low‑hazard industry exemption** – If your business falls into one of the **low‑hazard industry categories listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A**, you are likewise partially exempt. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  

**What you still must do**

* **Report all fatal injuries, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** to OSHA within the required time frames (within 8 hours for fatalities, 24 hours for hospitalizations, amputations, eye‑loss) even if you are exempt from the daily log. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
* **Keep injury records for at least five years** at the worksite. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

**Exceptions**

* Minor injuries that only require first aid are **not recorded** on OSHA Form 300 (they are excluded from recordkeeping). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  

So, if you meet the employee‑count or low‑hazard criteria, you are exempt from the daily OSHA 300/301 recordkeeping, but you must still report serious injuries as stated above and keep records for five years.

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
**Tax‑related records – what to keep and how long**

| What to keep | How long to keep it (from the IRS guidance) | Segment |
|--------------|---------------------------------------------|---------|
| **All documents that support each item of income or a deduction you report on a tax return** (e.g., receipts, invoices, bank statements, purchase orders, credit‑card statements, etc.) | Keep them **until the statute of limitations for that return expires** – the length of that period is the same as the period of limitations that applies to the underlying tax return (e.g., three years after the return is filed, or longer if a loss is carried forward). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Copies of the tax returns you file** (and information on how to produce them for amended returns or future calculations) | Keep copies **until the limitations period for that return expires** (the same period as above). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records** when you have employees (payroll, payroll tax filings, payroll tax payments, forms 941/944, etc.) | Keep them **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid—whichever is later**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Asset records** (purchase invoices, disposition documents, depreciation schedules, basis calculations) | Keep them until the **period of limitations expires for the year in which the property is disposed of**. That period is the same as the period of limitations for the tax return that reports the gain or loss from the disposal. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Injury‑related records – what to keep and how long**

| What to keep | How long to keep it | Segment |
|--------------|---------------------|---------|
| **OSHA injury and illness records** – the **Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)**, the **Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report)**, and the **Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)** | Keep them **at the worksite for at least five (5) years**. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** (treatment records, exposure logs, etc.) | Keep them for the **time period required for each specific type of record** (the length depends on the type of exposure; see OSHA regulations). | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker training records** (training logs, certifications, safety instructions) | Keep them available for **review by workers** as required by OSHA standards. The specific retention period is governed by OSHA standards for each type of training record. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

**Summary**

*For taxes* you must keep any document that substantiates income or deductions until the IRS’s applicable period of limitations ends (often 3‑5 years, but longer if you carry a loss). In addition, employment tax records have a flat 4‑year minimum, and asset records last until their disposal‑year limitations expire. Most of your routine business books, receipts, and invoices fall under this category.

*For injuries* you are required to retain OSHA Forms 300, 301 and 300A for at least five years at the workplace, and hold worker medical/exposure and training records for the periods mandated by OSHA regulations.

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

1. **Choose a legal structure**  
   • Decide whether you’ll operate as a **sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, or LLC**. The form you pick determines the tax return you file and the documentation you must keep. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
   • If you pick a corporation or LLC, file the required state paperwork (articles of incorporation/organization) with the Secretary of State and get a **Certificate of Incorporation/Organization**. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  

2. **Get a tax identification number**  
   • Apply for an **EIN (Employer Identification Number)** from the IRS (or use your SSN for a sole‑owner without employees). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  

3. **Set an accounting method and tax year**  
   • Choose a **cash basis or accrual basis** accounting method that shows income and expenses clearly for the tax year. See “Choosing an Accounting Method.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   • Decide whether your business will use a **calendar tax year (Jan 1‑Dec 31)** or a **fiscal year**; you adopt the year when you file your first return. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=53)  

4. **Open a separate business bank account**  
   • Keep business funds and personal funds completely separate. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

5. **Record every transaction**  
   • Use a **business checkbook** as the primary source of entries; record receipts, deposits, and disbursements daily. After each month you should **reconcile** your statement with your checkbook. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   • Keep a **summary of all business transactions** (journals and ledgers) so you can show gross income, deductions, and credits. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

6. **Maintain supporting documents**  
   • Save receipts, invoices, bank statements, credit‐card statements and a copy of every document that supports an expense or income entry. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
   • If you use electronic records, the system must preserve the records in legible format for the IRS. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

7. **Track deductible expenses**  
   • An expense is deductible if it is **ordinary (common in your field)** and **necessary (helpful and appropriate for the business)**. Typical start‑up costs that are fully deductible are up to $5,000 (with a phasing rule if costs exceed $50,000). [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  

8. **File your tax returns and make payments**  
   • All businesses except partnerships must file an annual **income tax return**.  
   • Sole proprietors or single‑member LLCs file Form 1040 with a Schedule C. Partnerships file Form 1065. Corporations file Form 1120 or 1120‑S. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  
   • Keep up with **payment deadlines**:  
     – **Income tax** and **self‑employment tax** are paid quarterly via **estimated payments** if you expect to owe $1,000+ (or $500+ for corporations). Use Form 1040‑ES. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9)  
     – If you have employees you must withhold **FICA, FUTA, and state taxes** and file the appropriate employer forms (W‑2, W‑3, 941, 940). [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)  
     – If you sell certain goods or use specific equipment, you may owe **excise taxes** reported on Forms 720 or 2290, and you may need to deposit those taxes before the return is due. [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)[[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  
   • If you miss a filing deadline, you can apply for a **six‑month extension** with Form 4868, but the tax due must still be paid when the return is filed. [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9)  

9. **Stay organized with a checklist**  
   • Create a **record‑keeping checklist** that mirrors the IRS requirement list (income, expenses, deductions, credits, supporting docs). Check it monthly to avoid errors and to have everything ready if the IRS audits. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

10. **Seek help and use free resources**  
   • Use **SBA, SBDC, or SCORE** for counseling on business plans and tax basics. Turn to IRS resources (Pub. 583, Pub. 505, Pub. 509) for guidance. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=53)[[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=49)  

By following these steps—choosing a structure, getting an EIN, setting an accounting method, keeping detailed records, filing the proper forms on time, and using IRS‑approved resources—you’ll be able to **start your business and keep your taxes organized**.

**Writing a Business Plan**

1. **Create the basic structure** – Start with a cover page that lists the company name, address, phone number, owners, and the date of the plan. Add a table of contents if you wish. Then write a brief executive summary (usually one or two paragraphs) that outlines the idea, funding needs, and key goals. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
2. **Follow the standard outline** – Include the following sections, each with its own heading and detailed content:
   * Describe Your Business – industry overview, competitive advantage, history and future projections.  
   * Describe Your Product(s) – marketability, purpose, uniqueness, manufacturing or service process, suppliers, quality assurance.  
   * Proprietary Information – patents, trademarks, copyrights, and any efforts to protect IP.  
   * Regulations – local, state, and federal licenses and permits required.  
   * Facility and Equipment – location, size, equipment needs, and future plans.  
   These are the core sections suggested in the plan guide. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  
3. **Financial section** – Provide the three key financial statements that lenders expect:  
   * 3‑Year Income Projection (monthly over three years).  
   * Statement of Cash Flow (projected inflow/outflow).  
   * Balance Sheet (assets, liabilities, equity as of a fixed date).  
   Also include historical statements if available and a summary of financial need. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
4. **Sources & Uses of Funds** – Draft a Sources & Uses Statement that lists all money you will receive and all money it will be spent on.  This helps lenders see how the capital will be deployed. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=21)  

**Setting Up Accounting**

1. **Open a business‑checking account** that is separate from any personal account.  Deposit all receipts and record all transactions on the business checkbook.  Withdraw personal funds only by checks payable to yourself.  Reconcile the account regularly so the book entries match the bank statement. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  
2. **Choose an accounting method** – Decide whether you will use the cash method, accrual method, or a combination.  The method you pick must be the same for all tax reporting and bookkeeping.  If you change later, you need IRS approval. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

| Item you should keep a record of | Why it matters (what the IRS looks for) | Source |

| **Gross receipts (all income)** – the total money you receive from your business | Needed to calculate your taxable income on Schedule C (Form 1040) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Ordinary & necessary business expenses** – e.g., rent, utilities, office supplies, insurance, advertising | These are deductible; you need receipts or other evidence for each expense | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=57)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Sales tax you collect from customers** | Sales tax is **not** deductible; you must report it separately so you don’t double‑count it as income | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Sales tax you pay on purchases** | Can be added to the basis of depreciable property (not a straight deduction) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Excise taxes** – e.g., fuel taxes on business‑use gas, environmental or transportation taxes | Must be reported on the appropriate form (e.g., Form 720, Form 2290); they may affect your deductible business expenses | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Fuel taxes you pay for business‑use fuel** | Generally included in the cost of the fuel and are not separately deductible | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Employment taxes** (if you have employees) – wages, tips, payroll tax withholdings | Must be reported on Forms 941, 940, 944, and included in your Schedule C | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |
| **Depreciation or Section 179 expense** for capital assets | Needed to spread out the cost of long‑term assets over several years | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=36) |
| **Receipts, canceled checks, invoices, or credit‑card slips** for every dollar you spend | The IRS requires proof that each deduction is real, ordinary, and necessary | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Detailed mileage logs if you use the standard mileage rate** – date, purpose, starting & ending odometer, miles | Required to claim the statutory mileage rate (e.g., 70 ¢/mile for 2025) | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Petty‑cash slips for small cash transactions** | Keeps a paper trail for amounts paid from a petty‑cash fund | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |

**What to track for travel expenses**

| Travel‑related item | What you can deduct | Documentation you need | Sources |
|---------------------|---------------------|------------------------|---------|
| **Mileage** for business driving | 70 ¢/mile (2025) when using the standard mileage rate, or actual expenses for gas, oil, tolls, parking, and maintenance | Mileage log (date, purpose, start/end odometer) | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Vehicle rental** | Only the portion used for business | Rental agreement and a per‑day log showing business use | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Lodging (hotel, motel, Airbnb, etc.)** | 100 % of the legitimate business portion | Hotel receipt or booking confirmation | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Meals** | Typically 50 % deductible for meals purchased while traveling for business | Restaurant receipt or a written record that satisfies the 50 % rule | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Tips for travel‑related services** | Deductible as part of the related expense | Tipping receipts or a written log of amounts | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Telephone/Internet usage on the trip** | Business‑use portion | Phone bill or a log showing business calls | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Parking and toll fees** | 100 % deductible; included with mileage if you use the standard rate | Parking receipt or toll tag record | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Cleaning and laundry while traveling** | 100 % deductible for business trips | Receipt from cleaning service | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Retirement or other unrelated trip expenses** | Not deductible | No record needed • | — |

**General record‑keeping tips**

1. Keep **separate records for business and personal** portions of any mixed expense.  
2. Store all receipts and supporting documents for **at least three years** (or longer if you’re self‑employed, the IRS requires up to 7 years in some cases).  
3. Use a **check‑disbursements journal** or spreadsheet to track every business check and credit‑card purchase.  
4. For small cash payments, make a **petty‑cash slip** and attach the receipt.  
5. For travel, keep a **detailed mileage log** and any written or electronic documentation that proves the business purpose.  

These records make it easier to complete the required tax forms (e.g., Schedule C, Form 1040‑ES for estimated tax, Form 941/940 for payroll) and prove that your deductions are ordinary, necessary, and well‑documented.

results.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
results.answer:
**If a customer cannot get through your front door**

1. **Make the entrance accessible** – Store entrances must provide a clear, 36‑inch‑wide passage that is free of obstacles and can be opened by any user.  Doors should be at least 36 inches wide and fit ADA standards; hardware that requires a tight grasp (e.g., round knobs, thumb‑latches) must be replaced or modified with a lever handle or clamp‑on lever.  If the current door is less than 36 in. (32 in. clear width when open) it must be widened or replaced, or a different mechanism such as a “swing‑clear” hinge that adds ~1½ in. of clearance may be used.  [[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)].

2. **Remove or modify barriers** – If a turnstile or security gate blocks access, remove the turnstile or replace it with an accessible gate that meets the 32‑inch minimum opening.  If other doors can serve as an entrance, provide a simple door handle or sign to designate it as an alternative entrance.  [[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)].

3. **Provide a nearby accessible entrance** – When the main front door is inaccessible, the business must either create a new accessible entrance (e.g., a ramp, lift, or slide‑by; see ramp and landing specifications) or designate an existing door as an alternative entrance.  The alternative entrance must be kept open during business hours and a sign must direct customers to it.  [[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)].

4. **Continue barrier removal as resources become available** – Even after an accessible entrance is provided, the owner is expected to continue removing barriers (e.g., steps, awnings brushing the sidewalk) whenever practicable.  This is part of the “readily achievable” requirement under ADA.  [[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)].

---

**If someone is hurt on site**

1. **Immediate first‑aid response** – Any exposure to bloodborne pathogens must trigger an immediate post‑exposure medical evaluation.  Emergency phone numbers and first‑aid supplies must be posted and readily accessible.  [[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=63)].

2. **Record the event** –  
   * One‑day or one‑incident forms: recordable injuries (except minor first‑aid only) go on OSHA **Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  
   * A supplemental **Form 301** (Injury and Illness Incident Report) is created for the recordable case.  
   * Changes: employers with 100+ employees in a high‑hazard industry must electronically submit the combined data to OSHA by **March 2 of the year following** the calendar year covered.  
   * All records (forms 300, 301, and exposure medical records) are retained onsite for at least **five years**.  
   * Fatalities must be reported to OSHA within **8 hours**; all in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye within **24 hours**.  [[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)].

3. **Maintain a safety program** – The business should have a safety and health program that includes procedures for reporting injuries, training workers on hazard identification, and conducting regular inspections.  The program should also list emergency procedures and provide contact information for emergency services.  [[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=13)].

4. **Follow OSHA guidelines** – After an injury, the business should review applicable OSHA standards (e.g., 29 CFR 1910.151 for medical services and first aid, 29 CFR 1904 for injury reporting) and ensure compliance with any corrective actions required.  [[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=63)[[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)].

---

**Summary**

- If a customer can’t reach the main door, make an accessible entrance (upgrade door width/hardware, remove/replace turnstiles, add a ramp or alternative door, provide directional signage, and continue barrier removal).  [[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)]  
- If someone is injured on the premises, provide immediate first aid, record the event on OSHA Form 300/301, retain records, and report fatalities or serious injuries within the required time frames while maintaining a comprehensive safety program.  [[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=63)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=13)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)]

results.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
results.answer:
**Why a safety program matters**

- A safety program is designed to *prevent* workplace injuries, illnesses, and deaths, which protects workers, their families, and the business from costly medical bills, workers’ compensation claims and lost productivity [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6).  
- Employers that treat safety as part of everyday operations are more likely to avoid future losses and to run a “sound business” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6).  
- OSHA recommends a proactive, step‑by‑step program that includes management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification, education, and continuous improvement.  This approach reduces the chance that a problem is only addressed after an incident occurs [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).  
- Beyond legal compliance, a good safety program boosts morale, improves employee retention, and can lower insurance premiums [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).

**Records you must keep**

| What to keep | Why it matters | Retention requirement |
|--------------|----------------|-----------------------|
| **OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)** – records each recordable injury or illness | Shows ongoing safety performance and identifies trends | Keep at the worksite for **at least five years** [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report)** – detailed supplemental record for each recordable case | Provides full details for investigation and regulatory review | Same five‑year retention as Form 300 [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)** – annual summary | Required for employers with 100+ workers in high‑hazard industries; used for OSHA’s recordkeeping regulations | Same five‑year retention as Forms 300/301 [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Fatality, hospitalization, amputation, loss‑of‑eye reports** – must be filed with OSHA within 8 hrs for fatalities and within 24 hrs for hospitalizations, amputations, or eye loss | OSHA enforcement requires timely filing | Included in the five‑year retention—these reports are part of Forms 300/301 [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** – e.g., lab test results, medical examinations | Required by OSHA and may be requested by employees | Retain for the period required for each specific type of record [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker training records** – proof of safety training, qualifications, and instruction | Needed to demonstrate compliance with OSHA training statutes and to provide workers access to their records | Keep accessible as required by OSHA [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Any other injury/illness documentation (e.g., incident reports, near‑miss logs, inspection reports)** – supports investigation and corrective action | Helps maintain continuous improvement and is useful for audits | Keep as long as required for business or legal purposes [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

**Key deadlines**

- **Electronic submission** of forms 300 and 301 to OSHA is required *by March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered* for eligible employers (100+ workers in high‑hazard industries) [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

These records are the foundation of a compliant safety program: they keep your business safe, demonstrate good faith to regulators, and help you improve safety performance over time.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
**How long you must keep tax records**

* Keep any records that support an item of income or deduction on your tax return until the “period of limitations” for that return runs out. The period of limitations is the time the IRS has to assess additional tax or you have the time to amend the return to claim a credit or refund. The specific limits for different types of returns are listed in the IRS table of periods of limitations (see Table 3).  
  – Example: for most individual income‑tax returns the limitation is 3 years after the return is filed unless a larger error exists.  

* If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.  
  – (“Employment taxes. If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.”) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* Records that relate to property (e.g., to calculate depreciation, basis, or gain/loss when you sell or otherwise dispose of the property) should be kept **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property**.  
  – (“Assets. Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition.”) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* It is also advisable to keep copies of every filed tax return itself, as they are needed to prepare future returns and to calculate any amended return.  
  – (“Keep copies of your filed tax returns. They help in preparing future tax returns and making computations if you file an amended return.”) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Summary**:  
- For ordinary income‑tax items, retain records for the applicable period of limitations (usually 3 years, or longer if the tax under‑reported a significant amount).  
- For employment taxes, keep records for 4 years.  
- For property‑related records, retain them through the limitation period of the year you dispose of the property.  

These are the specific retention periods provided in the IRS guidance.

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **Monitor your business’s progress** – Good records let you see whether the business is improving, which items sell best, and what changes are needed, increasing the likelihood of success. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

2. **Prepare accurate financial statements** – Records are required to build income‑statement (profit‑loss) and balance‑sheet reports that help you manage the business and satisfy banks or creditors. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

3. **Identify the source of receipts** – When money or property comes in, records show whether the income is taxable or non‑taxable and separate business receipts from personal ones, which is essential for correct tax reporting. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **Track deductible expenses** – Recording expenses as they occur prevents you from forgetting them when you file the tax return, ensuring you claim all allowed deductions. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

5. **Prepare and support tax returns** – All items you report on your tax return must be backed by records. The IRS may inspect your books, and a complete set will speed up any examination. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

6. **Meet IRS retention rules** – The IRS requires records to be available for inspection. The same rules apply to electronic records that replace hard copies, which must keep the same level of detail and accessibility. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

7. **Provide evidence for business and non‑business purposes** – Besides tax needs, insurers, creditors, and other entities may require these records for longer than the IRS mandates. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

8. **Maintain proper bookkeeping systems** – Whether you use a single‑entry or double‑entry system, keeping journals, ledgers, checkbooks, and inventory summaries helps keep your books balanced and audit‑ready. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

9. **Include required supporting documents** – Acceptable statements from banks, credit cards, and electronic funds transfers must show the check number, amount, payee, and posting date, and should be accompanied by receipts, invoices, or sales slips to prove a deduction. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

10. **Adjust for inventory and specific business needs** – If you hold inventory, you must keep inventory records and use an accounting method that clearly reflects income. If the business has multiple entities, separate books are required. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

By keeping these records, you not only satisfy legal and tax obligations but also gain a clearer picture of your business’s financial health and operational efficiency.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The IRS lets you pick one of several accounting methods for a business, but you must use the same method for both calculating taxable income and keeping your books, and you normally choose it when you file your first business tax return (Schedule C with Form 1040). Here’s how to decide which one is appropriate for you: | Accounting Method | When it’s usually used | What it means | Key rules from the IRS docs | |-------------------|------------------------|--------------|-----------------------------| | **Cash method** | • Small‑to‑mid‑size businesses that do not keep inventory.
• Businesses that want the simplest record‑keeping and usually collect cash quickly. | Income is reported in the year you receive the money; expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year you pay them. | • You must use the cash method for both income and expense reporting unless you have inventory, in which case you must use accrual for the inventory portion (but the rules treat the whole method as cash if you mix the two) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).

• Businesses that want to match income with the expenses that created it. | Income is reported when earned, regardless of when paid; expenses are reported when incurred. | • If your business sells products or manufactures goods, you generally must keep an inventory and use accrual for purchases and sales of inventory [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).

• When you use a mix of cash and accrual to get the best picture of your income but keep the method consistent. | You can combine elements of cash, accrual, and special methods, provided the combination clearly shows your income. | • If you mix cash and accrual, the combination is treated as cash for reporting purposes [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).
• Special methods (depreciation, amortization, depletion, etc.) are allowed for particular items and are explained in detailed IRS **Consider how you receive money**. * If you get paid when the work is done, an accrual method will match income to the payment period. * If you get paid quickly and not much is owed to you, a cash system. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) * The accrual method requires double‑entry bookkeeping runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the two‑step process outlined in the handbook:

**1. Conduct a routine self‑inspection**  
- **Use the handbook’s checklists** to look for common hazards in your industry. The checklists are a starting point for identifying what might be wrong and where to start fixing it. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
- **Record findings** on the same form, noting whether hazards were found, how they’re being controlled, and whether controls are still working. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
- **Involve workers**. Workers help spot hazards, suggest controls, and can be assigned to implement and evaluate those controls. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  

**2. Analyze and act on the results**  
- **Match any identified hazards to OSHA standards** that apply to your business. If a standard covers a hazard, follow its requirements; if it doesn’t, use the general‑duty clause. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)  
- **Compile all data** (checklists, injury/illness records, training logs, maintenance records) to see where the problems cluster. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
- **Find solutions**. Once you know where hazards exist, look to the handbook’s “additional resources” links or OSHA’s website for control options. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

**Additional support**  
- If the self‑inspection shows many hazards or you’re uncertain about compliance, **contact an OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program**. Consultants can help you identify hazards and fix them. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)  

**Keep the program ongoing**  
- Perform self‑inspections regularly; update your hazard list and controls as work or equipment changes.  
- Review the safety post‑on itself: keep the OSHA poster, notice of any citations, and emergency numbers posted. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=13)  

By following these steps—planning, inspecting, analyzing, acting, and repeating—you’ll maintain a safer workplace and stay in line with OSHA guidance.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash accounting and accrual accounting are the two main ways you can report business income and expenses for tax purposes.

**Cash method**

- You report income when you actually receive the money (or it becomes available to you – “constructive receipt”).  
  *Example:* a client sends a check on December 30 2024 that you get on January 4 2025 is counted as 2025 income [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you actually pay them.  
- It is the simpler method and is permitted for many sole proprietors who don’t keep inventory. However, if you have inventory you’re required to use accrual to record sales and purchases of that inventory but you can still use cash for other income and expenses that don’t involve inventory [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

**Accrual method**

- You report income in the year it is earned, even if the payment comes later, because the earning “events have occurred.”  
  *Example:* you sell a computer on December 28 2025, bill the customer in early January 2026, and get paid in February 2026, but the computer sale is 2025 income because the sale event happened in 2025 [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses in the year they are incurred, regardless of when you pay them.  
  *Example:* you buy office supplies in December 2025, receive the bill and pay it in January 2026, but you can deduct the expense in 2025 because the liability was fixed and economic performance occurred that year [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
- Accrual is required when you keep an inventory of goods, raw materials, or supplies that you intend to sell, because you must match the cost of those items with the revenue they generate [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) and also covered in Segment 4.

**Key differences summarized**

| Item | Cash method | Accrual method |
|------|-------------|----------------|
| Income timing | when money is received or constructively available | when earned (sales are made, services performed) |
| Expense timing | when money is paid | when incurred (purchase of goods, services, or capital) |
| Inventory requirement | not required for most sole‑prop businesses; if you have inventory, use accrual for those items | required for any business with inventory; inventory must be recorded at both the beginning and end of the year |
| Example of constructive receipt | a check sent December 30 but received January 4 is still 2025 income | – |
| Example of income earned but payment late | – | a December sale of computer counted in 2025 even if paid 2026 | 

These rules are the ones the IRS uses to let you pick the method that best matches how your business operates. If you keep inventory, you normally must use accrual; otherwise you can choose cash unless the IRS has a reason to require the other method.

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes – you can deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while you’re traveling for business.  
The deduction covers several categories of cost:

* **Meals and lodging** – If the trip is overnight or long enough that you need to sleep to perform your work, you may deduct the cost of meals and lodging.  You can use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance.  For most meals you may deduct only **50 %** of the cost【Segment 1】.  Lodging can be fully deducted if it is for a business trip【Segment 1】.  
* **Car and truck expenses** – Any rental car you use while away from home can be deducted in its entirety, but only for the portion used for business.  For your own vehicle you may deduct either the actual cost of operation (fuel, maintenance, insurance, parking, tolls, etc.) or the standard mileage rate.  For 2025 the standard mileage rate is **70 ¢ per business mile**【Segment 5】.  
* **Other transportation** – Taxi, commuter‑bus, limousine fares and other local transportation between the airport (or train station) and your hotel, or between the hotel and your work location, are deductible【Segment 3】.  
* **Telephone, fax and other communication** – Phone calls made for business while traveling are deductible【Segment 1】.  
* **Tips** – You may deduct tips paid for any service that appears in the travel‑expense list【Segment 1】.  
* **Baggage and shipping** – Sending baggage, samples or display material between your regular and temporary work locations is deductible【Segment 3】.  

If you reimburse employees for these travel expenses, the amount you reimburse can be deducted, but the manner of deduction depends on whether the reimbursement is under an accountable or non‑accountable plan (see Pub. 15)【Segment 1】.  

All deductions must be ordinary and necessary, and any personal portion of the expense must be separated and is not deductible (e.g., commuting miles to a regular place of business)【Segment 1】【Segment 5】.
